title: 4 days Upper Lower split Program review
summary: He reviews a viewer's (Philip) six-day ABCD rotation built around deadlift, overhead press, squat and bench days, judging it as a bodybuilder. He criticises fixed rep schemes like 2x5 and 3x5, too-low rows reps, low main-lift volume (especially bench and OHP) shifted to dumbbell variations, supinated rows, flyes, and 8-20 rep windows, while praising the heavy-then-light curl pairing, calf volume and autoregulation. He closes with general advice on writing your own program and on exercises you keep skipping.

claims.claim: Strength and size are correlated only to an extent, less than people think; he reviews programs as a bodybuilder, not a powerlifter.
Rotating a six-day ABCD program so two main lifts get trained twice in alternating weeks is a smart approach.
A 1x5 deadlift is good for strength but not hypertrophy; he'd prefer 3x3 or 3x4, and a 3x3 at a challenging weight is a lot of deadlift tonnage.
Fixed schemes like 2x5 or 5x5 are flawed: hitting 5 then 5 means you either undersold the first set or oversold the second; prefer rep schemes that evolve as you progress (e.g. 3x4-6 instead of 3x5).
He advises against supinated and mixed-grip rows (and pulls) to avoid tearing a bicep.
Barbell rows don't benefit from low reps; do a minimum of 8, aiming for 8-12, controlling the negative and letting the back stretch.
Weighted chin-ups work well in low rep ranges while unweighted chin-ups suit higher reps, so rows and chins rep ranges should be swapped in this program.
Two rowing movements plus chin-ups in one session borders on overkill, but if your back can handle it, more volume generally gives better gains.
He sees little synergy between deadlifts and biceps and prefers dedicated arm days, but without an arm day, deadlift day is the realistic place for biceps.
3x8 (or 3x5-6) is very low volume for biceps; pairing a heavy low-rep barbell curl with lighter high-rep preacher curls for more tension is a smart combination, and up to 5 sets is good volume.
Don't stop sets early because the pump feels bad; do the work regardless. He never gets leg pumps and still squats.
3x5 is low volume for overhead press; he does 3x5 plus 3x2-5 on his overhead press day.
3x6-12 is a good rep range for shrugs.
Write your own program and then get others to help balance it; the knowledge from writing your own beats buying a 'perfect' one, since nobody else knows you, regardless of their diplomas.
Fixed rep ranges are acceptable for front squats because it's a technical lift; 3x6 is a fine scheme.
Never go below 8 reps on lunges or good mornings; they don't respond well to intensity and the risk-reward isn't there for the knee or lower back.
Calves need volume: muscles called stubborn (calves, forearms) are ones used all day, whereas biceps and chest blow up early because they're never stimulated otherwise.

You can skip calf work in your novice phase while focusing on compounds, but after that train them; he never trained calves in nine years and ended up with massive quads and small calves that grow slowly.
3x5 on flat bench (15 reps) is not enough even at twice a week; even as a bodybuilder he hits a bare minimum of about 60 working reps on bench, and would move this to at least 5x5.
He dislikes dumbbell flyes with extended arms: more dangerous than rewarding.

Shifting pressing volume from flat bench to dumbbell variations likely costs gains; more flat bench and less dumbbell pressing would be better, and the same for barbell OHP over seated dumbbell press.
An 8-20 rep window gives too much room for laziness; with an appropriate weight and enough rest, reps shouldn't drop from 20 to 8. Use 10-15 for four sets, or 14-20 if pushing toward 20.

If after six months you keep skipping part of your program, ask whether it's laziness (then move it earlier to force yourself) or because you instinctively know it's not needed (then remove it, since it only creates guilt and mental stress).
For deadlifts he'd keep a minimum of two working sets, ideally 4x3 at a relatively challenging weight, or a few challenging sets followed by a back-off he can rep.
Alternate barbell rows and one-arm dumbbell rows across sessions, doing one with intensity and the other with higher volume, to keep training fresh.
He is too weak to do weighted chin-ups himself but thinks they are amazing.
This program could use more direct trap work, more curls and more long-head triceps work, though trap development is very genetic.
